title: Concurrent requests bypass approval and immutability rules
actual: An edit paused after validation overwrote an approved $10 receipt with a waiting $99 receipt. An approval paused after validation approved a newly edited $200 total with only one approval. A paused void subsequently voided an approved receipt. All three competing writes returned HTTP 200.
expected: Exactly one conflicting transition commits. The stale operation returns 409; approved values remain immutable; amounts above $150 require two distinct approvers.
reproduction: Create a complete $10 receipt. Pause one operation immediately before the real changeExpense adapter. Complete the competing approve/edit/void request, then release the paused operation. Tests exercise three valid request interleavings against the migrated database.
impact: Approvers can authorize an amount they never reviewed, two-step approval can be bypassed, and approved entries can be altered or voided.
recommendation: Validate the expected version, current status, amount and permitted transition inside the same transaction as the write. Reject stale versions atomically and record the committed decision against its reviewed version.

title: Malformed money is silently converted to a different amount
actual: 12,34 becomes 123400 cents ($1,234.00); 1 2.34 and 1$2.34 become 1234 cents ($12.34). These values pass cleanExpense validation.
expected: Malformed grouping, internal spaces and misplaced currency symbols receive a validation error rather than a financially different value.
reproduction: Call cleanExpense with an otherwise valid receipt and total 12,34, 1 2.34 or 1$2.34.
impact: Typing or locale mistakes can silently overstate expenses.
recommendation: Validate the entire amount format before removing permitted currency/grouping characters. Define supported locales explicitly and keep integer-cent storage.

title: Saving an incomplete missing receipt falsely marks its charge as matched
actual: Import a $10 charge, then save its missing expense without a receipt, lost reason or category. The expense becomes draft, its Amex line becomes matched, and missingNow falls from 1/$10 to 0/$0.
expected: A charge with neither a receipt nor a lost-receipt reason remains missing and stays in the missing count and amount.
reproduction: Import R1 for $10 on 2026-11-05. PUT its generated expense with the same date/total and empty receiptUrl, lostReason and category. GET statements for 2026-11.
impact: Accounting's missing-receipt control understates outstanding documentation.
recommendation: Derive receipt presence from the actual attachment/lost reason instead of treating every linked non-missing workflow status as uploaded. Keep counts, line status and reconciliation selection consistent.

title: Changed statement references retain invalid amount and card matches
actual: Reimporting R1 at $11 retained its link to a $10 expense. Changing R1's digits from 12345 to 54321 retained its original card link instead of selecting the second holder's card.
expected: A refreshed statement line must either still satisfy card/amount/date match invariants or become an explicit reconciliation exception requiring review.
reproduction: Save and import a matched $10 receipt. Reimport the same reference with amount 11; independently repeat with changed card digits. Inspect statement line, linked expense and card.
impact: A charge can appear reconciled against the wrong amount or cardholder.
recommendation: Revalidate existing links when imported match keys change. Preserve approved expense history and flag/unmatch inconsistencies rather than silently rewriting approved accounting records.

title: A nonexistent customer satisfies completeness before its reference is discarded
actual: A Customer lunch with a fabricated 24-character customer ID, a name and attendees returns 201/waiting. Postgres stores a null customer reference, while the supplied customer name remains.
expected: Reject nonexistent or unauthorized customer references; a category requiring a customer must not enter approval with a null customer reference.
reproduction: POST a Customer lunch using customerId 0000000000000000000003e7, customerName Does not exist and two attendees.
impact: Customer-linked expenses can be approved and reported without a valid underlying customer.
recommendation: Resolve and authorize the customer on the server, derive its display name from that record, and validate completeness on the record that will actually be persisted.

title: Deleting a category leaves approved receipts invalid under the replacement rules
actual: An approved Fuel receipt moved to Customer lunch through category deletion remains approved with no customer or attendees.
expected: An administrative replacement must preserve valid approved history or require missing fields and reapproval under the new category's requirements.
reproduction: Approve a Fuel receipt. DELETE the Fuel category with Customer lunch as replaceWith. Inspect the expense's category, status, customer and approval.
impact: Category administration can create approved expenses that fail the module's ordinary approval prerequisites.
recommendation: Keep archived categories for approved history, or define an audited migration that invalidates approval when the new category changes required information.

title: Concurrent different-ID saves bypass the duplicate warning
actual: Two concurrent requests for the same holder/day/amount, with different IDs and no confirmRepeat, both return 201 and create two live expenses.
expected: One save succeeds; the other receives the repeat warning until the holder explicitly confirms a second purchase.
reproduction: Pause both requests before addExpense, after each passed sameDayAmount. Release both and inspect the two responses and persisted row count.
impact: Double submission can overstate expense totals without the intended duplicate confirmation.
recommendation: Serialize duplicate detection and insert per holder/day/amount in one transaction; preserve the explicitly authorized Save anyway path.

title: Amex lookup failure removes the matched-charge protection
actual: Injecting a linkedLine database read failure lets the holder void a matched charge with HTTP 200; voidedAt is saved.
expected: An unavailable reconciliation lookup blocks the protected mutation with an error and leaves the matched expense unchanged.
reproduction: Save a receipt, import its matching Amex charge, inject one linkedLine read failure and POST the holder's void request.
impact: A transient dependency failure allows accounting data changes that the normal matched-charge rule forbids. The same helper protects date/amount edits.
recommendation: Distinguish unlinked from lookup unavailable. Fail the protected write when the lookup is unavailable while Postgres reconciliation is enabled.

title: A monthly ledger silently truncates after 5,000 expenses
actual: A seeded 5,001-row month at $10 per row returns 5,000 expenses totaling $50,000 instead of $50,010. The response exposes no total count or continuation metadata. UI totals and export use this returned list.
expected: All rows and exact totals remain accessible through pagination/server aggregates, and an export covers the requested accounting scope without silent truncation.
reproduction: Insert 5,001 receipts for one month. GET expenses?scope=all&month=2026-11 and compare returned count and sum with the database.
impact: Large months understate the ledger and exported spend.
recommendation: Return explicit pagination and total aggregates; provide a complete scoped export path instead of using a capped list as the ledger.

title: The concurrent-save fallback can disclose another holder's expense
actual: Two different holders racing on one new receipt ID receive 201 and 200. The losing holder receives the other holder's expense object, including its card/holder data, rather than 409.
expected: The ID belongs to exactly one holder. Both the initial lookup and post-conflict fallback enforce ownership before returning an expense.
reproduction: Start two authenticated holders with active cards and the same new receipt ID. Gate both just before addExpense so both initial lookups see no row, then release them.
impact: A specifically timed ID collision can cross the receipt ownership boundary. It requires the same chosen/known 24-character ID, not an ordinary random collision.
recommendation: Check again.userId against the authenticated holder before returning the fallback object, and handle duplicate-key races without exposing the conflicting record.

title: Malformed dates are truncated and tomorrow is accepted by the shared validator
actual: 2026-11-05garbage is silently saved as 2026-11-05. With today fixed at 2026-11-20, 2026-11-21 is accepted by cleanExpense even though the date picker sets max=today.
expected: Validate the complete date string. The form and server should enforce the same documented cutoff.
reproduction: Call cleanExpense with the two dates and today 2026-11-20.
impact: Malformed API input changes accounting dates silently. Tomorrow acceptance is a policy discrepancy to confirm: the server explicitly allows a one-day grace period, so this portion is not presented as a settled business-rule defect.
recommendation: Require exact YYYY-MM-DD input before normalization and document whether the intentional one-day grace period is required. Apply the chosen cutoff consistently.

title: An approval-queue outage is shown as an empty queue
actual: When scope=waiting returns 503, both desktop and phone show Waiting for me 0/$0 and Nothing is waiting for you, with no error.
expected: Show a queue-load error and retry affordance; do not represent failed loading as a verified empty queue.
reproduction: Mock only the waiting-list response to 503, leave ordinary expenses successful and open Waiting for me. Browser tests and saved screenshots reproduce both viewports.
impact: Approvers can believe there are no pending receipts while the queue is unavailable.
recommendation: Track waiting-list loading/error separately and show an empty state only after a successful request.
